notes:
- The **Rollback snapshots** card lists the saved snapshots again. A display
  that had taken three or more of them -- by now, every display -- showed
  "None yet" even though the snapshots were there and an undo would have
  worked: the page was cutting the list off before it could be read. The
  snapshots themselves were never touched, and a rollback still worked from
  the command line the whole time; this only restores the page's view of them.
- The **Screen rotation** setting now uses the same words as Windows --
  **Landscape**, **Portrait**, **Landscape (flipped)**, **Portrait (flipped)**
  -- instead of "90 left / 90 right". It matches what the same panel was set to
  under Windows, so there is nothing to translate. Nothing about how a display
  rotates changed; only the labels.
- **Machines converted from Windows now come up on whatever Wi-Fi they were on,
  open networks included.** The installer keeps the exact connection it used to
  reach the network rather than assuming a WPA2 password -- so an open network,
  or a WPA3 one, is no longer left unable to rejoin the network it was installed
  over. (This is in the installer, so it applies to new conversions, not to a
  display that is already running.)
- **Screen rotation now holds across a reboot, and Portrait means Portrait.**
  Two fixes for the rotation setting, both found on a converted display:
  - **It sticks now, even without a touchscreen.** On a marketing or menu board
    (no touchscreen at all), setting a rotation turned the screen but did not
    survive the next reboot -- it came back Landscape -- because a "no
    touchscreen" result was mistaken for a failure and the setting was never
    saved. Whether the screen actually turned is now what counts, so the
    rotation is written down and re-applied on every boot.
  - **Portrait and Portrait (flipped) were the wrong way round.** A panel that
    Windows called "Portrait" only came up right-side-up if you chose "Portrait
    (flipped)". They are corrected, so the label matches the physical result --
    choose Portrait for a Windows-Portrait panel.
- **The page-reload settings moved to the Page tab and got clearer.** Two
  separate things now, instead of one vague "auto-reload":
  - **Idle reset** returns the display to its page after it has been idle for a
    while -- a kiosk going back to its login screen. A normal reload.
  - **Auto-reload** does a hard refresh to pick up a new version of the web app,
    on whichever trigger you choose: after the display has been idle, or at a set
    time of day. By default it only reloads while the page is reachable, so it
    never refreshes onto a blank screen.
- **Pinch-to-zoom can be turned off, and is off by default.** Under Permissions:
  a customer at a touch display can no longer pinch the page out of shape and
  leave it that way for the next person. Turn it back on for a display where
  pinching is wanted.
This release ships with a new OS image (os 1.4.6). The software is delivered as
normal signed components; the image is what carries the parts a component cannot
install for itself — the first-boot gate and the ScreenConnect first-boot
enrolment — so a machine gets the full behaviour only when it is installed from
this image.
- **A fresh display checks for updates before it shows the setup screen.** On the
  very first boot it briefly says "checking for updates" and applies anything
  waiting, so a new install lands current instead of coming up on the image's
  baked-in software and only catching up hours later at its first update window.
  It never strands the boot: no network, or nothing to fetch, and it goes
  straight on to setup.
- **The installer no longer asks for a Display name.** The setup screens now show
  the machine's own hostname (ds-hwid) instead. A name typed at install time was
  only ever a second label for the same box; the admin page can still set a
  friendly name whenever you want one.
- **A reinstalled display that belongs to an account waits for the owner to
  approve it.** Reinstalling or resetting a claimed display mints a new device
  key; rather than trusting whoever reflashed it, the server holds the new key
  pending and the account owner approves the change from their own portal — no
  call to us. A standalone display (in nobody's account) still just pairs, so a
  forgotten admin password is always recoverable by reinstalling.
- **Wake-on-LAN is enabled on supported wired machines (x86).** A display on
  hardware we control can be woken from the LAN after it is powered off. It
  detects and reports whether the machine is even a candidate — firmware still
  has to keep the NIC powered in S5 — so you can tell which displays WoL can
  actually reach rather than finding out a BIOS setting did nothing.
- **Restarting the browser now waits until the page is back before it reports
  done**, the same way reboot and update already do, instead of returning while
  the screen is still black.
- **A freshly enrolled display restarts its ScreenConnect agent once, by
  itself.** ConnectWise's installer can leave the service dead a few seconds
  after first boot, which is why a new convert so often needed the admin page's
  "Restart service" pressed by hand before it appeared in the console. The
  display now does that press automatically, once, after the agent has settled.
- **A ScreenConnect agent that installs but dies is now brought back
  automatically.** ConnectWise's own postinstall sometimes leaves the service
  dead a few seconds after a fresh convert first comes up -- which is why a new
  display so often had to have "Restart service" pressed by hand before it
  appeared in the console. Every display now checks on each update pass whether
  its agent is installed-but-stopped and restarts it, retrying until it stays up.
  Because it rides the ordinary software update, a display already in the field
  self-heals at its next check -- no reflash -- and it keeps watch afterwards, so
  an agent that dies later comes back on its own. (Delivered as a component; a
  display gets it on whichever channel it tracks.)
- **First-boot enrolment retries until the agent is actually running**, instead
  of trusting a single delayed restart. On a machine installed from a new image,
  the agent comes up within a minute or two of first boot and is confirmed to
  stay up before the enrolment step stands down.
- **The installer now asks which updates a display should receive.** Stable
  (strongly recommended) or Testing (risky). Stable stays the default and is what
  a store display should be on; Testing is the opt-in for a bench display that
  needs unreleased software. The from-Windows converter shows the same choice,
  and a batch file that says nothing still installs Stable exactly as before.
- **The "checking for updates" screen no longer has a red border.** That red edge
  means "the page is unreachable"; it belongs on a customer's page, not on one of
  our own setup screens, which already say in words what the network is doing. It
  was suppressed on the welcome and startup screens but had been missed on this
  one.
- **A standalone display no longer shows the "belongs to an existing account"
  notice.** A layout bug left that notice on screen on every display from the
  moment it loaded -- including displays that are in nobody's account. Now it
  appears only when a display genuinely was reinstalled while claimed to an
  account, and then it takes the place of the "link to an account" box rather
  than sitting beside it. The wording is shorter, and it shows the display's
  device key so you can check it against the one your account shows.
- **The device key and the account pairing code are now clearly different
  things.** The 12-character value derived from a display's key is called the
  "device key" everywhere -- the setup screen, the admin page (it had been
  mislabeled "pairing code"), and the reinstalled notice -- and the account
  pairing code stays the account pairing code. One is how you confirm a display's
  identity; the other is how you link a new display to an account.
- **You can clear a display's page now, and it drops back to the welcome
  screen.** Leaving the page URL blank in the admin used to be rejected, so once
  a page was set the only move was to point it somewhere else. Now a blank URL
  clears it and the display shows its welcome screen again -- and the admin shows
  a cleared page as an empty box and "Welcome screen", not the literal
  "about:blank" or an internal address.
- **Pinch-to-zoom is held at the browser level, not just the page.** The lock
  (off by default) put a no-zoom viewport on the customer's page, but on a touch
  panel WebKit ignored it and a customer could still pinch the page out of shape.
  The display now also snaps the zoom back whenever the lock is on, so a pinch no
  longer sticks.
- **Pinch-to-zoom is now actually held on a touch panel.** The lock (off by
  default) stops a customer pinching the page out of shape and leaving it that
  way. WebKit on a touch panel ignored the page-level block, and a pinch scales
  the page rather than the browser zoom, so the earlier browser-zoom clamp missed
  it too. The display now intercepts the two-finger gesture itself, before WebKit
  can assemble it into a zoom. Proven on a real touch panel: with the lock on a
  pinch does nothing and a one-finger scroll still works; with the lock off pinch
  zooms normally.
